title: TCP Friendly Rate Control (TFRC): Protocol Specification
summary: Specifies TCP Friendly Rate Control, a congestion control mechanism for unicast flows in best-effort networks. It is reasonably fair when competing with TCP flows but varies throughput much less over time, which suits streaming media where a smooth sending rate matters. It replaced RFC 3448.

plainLanguage.summary: TCP Friendly Rate Control (TFRC) sets a sending rate using reports about packet loss and round-trip time. It aims to share network capacity fairly with TCP while changing speed less sharply, which can help applications that need a steadier flow.

questions: how does tfrc differ from tcp congestion control
what is the tcp throughput equation
subtitle: A congestion-control method that shares bandwidth with TCP while keeping its sending rate steadier.

tldr.problem: TCP can cut its sending rate sharply after packet loss. Applications such as streaming media may need a smoother rate while still sharing bandwidth fairly with TCP.
tldr.mechanism: The receiver estimates packet-loss events and reports them. The sender combines that rate with its round-trip-time estimate in a TCP throughput equation to choose a sending rate.
tldr.outcome: TFRC is reasonably fair to TCP and has less throughput variation, but it reacts more slowly to changes in available bandwidth. RFC 5348 obsoletes RFC 3448 and updates RFC 4342.

today: RFC 5348 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2008. It obsoletes RFC 3448 and updates RFC 4342.

sections.title: What TFRC Is Designed to Do
sections.content:
TFRC is a congestion-control mechanism for unicast traffic in a best-effort Internet. It is designed for flows that compete with TCP. The RFC calls a flow reasonably fair when its rate is generally within a factor of two of a TCP flow under the same conditions.

TFRC produces less variation in throughput than TCP, but it responds more slowly when available bandwidth changes. The RFC therefore recommends it when an application needs a smooth sending rate, rather than simply transferring as much data as quickly as possible. TFRC does not define a complete transport protocol, packet format, or reliability mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: TFRC is a rule for how quickly one sender should transmit data. It aims to share capacity fairly with TCP, while changing the rate less sharply.

sections.title: The Feedback Loop and Rate Equation
sections.content:
The receiver estimates the rate of loss events and sends that information to the sender. The sender also measures round-trip time (RTT), the time for data and feedback to travel between endpoints. It uses the loss rate, RTT, and segment size in a TCP throughput equation to calculate a permitted rate.

The sender limits that result using the receiver's reported rate, then adjusts its transmissions to match. Before it has observed loss, it uses an initial slow-start phase. The RFC specifies the equation and the measurements it requires, but leaves packet formats to the transport protocol that uses TFRC.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver reports how often packets are lost. The sender combines that report with the round-trip time to calculate a sending rate.

sections.title: Sender Feedback and Timeouts
sections.content:
Data packets carry increasing sequence numbers, timestamps, and normally the sender's current RTT estimate. Feedback reports carry the timestamp of the latest received packet, receiver delay, receive rate, and loss-event rate. The sender uses these values to update its RTT estimate and permitted sending rate.

If feedback stops, the nofeedback timer eventually expires and the sender reduces its allowed rate. The timer is set for four RTTs after an RTT estimate is available; before the first RTT sample its initial value is two seconds. TFRC also limits bursts after idle or data-limited periods to no more than one RTT's worth of packets.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender updates its rate when it receives feedback. If feedback stops, it lowers the permitted rate and limits how much data it can send in a burst.

sections.title: How the Receiver Measures Loss
sections.content:
The receiver treats a packet as lost after three packets with higher sequence numbers arrive. A late packet can fill the gap, so the receiver can recalculate its loss estimate. For an ECN-capable connection, a marked packet counts as a congestion event as soon as it arrives.

The receiver groups losses that fall within one RTT into a loss event, then measures the lengths of the intervals between events. It averages recent intervals, giving newer intervals more weight, and derives the loss-event rate from that average. The RFC recommends averaging eight intervals.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver tracks gaps in packet sequence numbers. It groups nearby losses into events and uses the spacing between events to estimate congestion.

sections.title: Security and Status
sections.content:
TFRC is a congestion-control mechanism rather than a complete transport protocol, so the protocol using it must provide most security protections. Spoofed feedback could cause a sender to change its rate. A transport protocol should accept feedback only from the intended receiver.

A dishonest receiver could claim that fewer packets were lost and gain an unfair rate. The RFC describes using a nonce that the receiver must echo as a possible defense; the details depend on the transport protocol. RFC 5348 is a Proposed Standard, obsoletes RFC 3448, and updates RFC 4342.
sections.plainLanguage: A sender must know that its feedback really came from the receiver. Otherwise, false reports could make it send at an unfair rate.
